column2: The Goddess wears the half-moon and jewelled earrings; her braid is lovely, her eyes are large, and she is adorned with three eyes.
She holds a rosary of letters, her hands shine with bracelets, her fingers bear golden rings, and her hands gleam with bangles.
Fair-skinned, clad in white garments, shining on a lotus seat, with a saffron dot as her tilaka and her head adorned with the moon,
radiant as lightning, her breasts rising beneath a bodice of costly cloth, she holds excellent weapons in eight lofty arms.
The gods said: Victory to you, Durga, great queen; victory to you, who love your own people. Salutation again and again to you, Shiva, protector of the three worlds.
No asura woman, naga woman, gandharva woman or danava woman in the three worlds is such as that charming one.
Therefore fitness to enjoy her befits you alone; for she is the jewel of women, and you, lord, are the jewel of men."
Hearing what Chanda and Munda said, the great asura sent a messenger named Sugriva to her.
Go, messenger, to the snowy mountain; some beautiful woman is there. She must be brought with effort, after telling her my words.
Instructed thus by him, Sugriva, the excellent danava, went to the Himalaya and spoke to the Mother of the world, the great Goddess.
The messenger said: "Goddess, the daitya Shumbhasura and his younger brother Nishumbha are famed in the three worlds for great strength and valour.
I am a messenger sent by him to come into your presence. Hear now, queen of the gods, what he has said:
'Having conquered Indra and the others in battle, I have taken away their jewels; I myself enjoy the gods' share given in sacrifice by the gods and others.
I regard you as the jewel among women, above all jewels; so worship me or my younger brother with the delights born of love.'"
Hearing these words of Shumbha spoken by the messenger, Mahamaya, the beloved of the lord of beings, said:
Salutation to the giver of liberation; salutation again and again to the supreme Mother. Salutation to you who bring about the origin, continuance and end of the whole of worldly existence.
The Goddess said: "You speak the truth, messenger; nothing false is said. But I made one vow earlier; hear it from me.
He who shakes off my pride, he who conquers me in battle — him and no other I resolve to take as my husband; this is certain.
So tell my words to Shumbha and Nishumbha; let him do here whatever is fitting."
Hearing the Goddess's words thus, the danava named Sugriva went and informed the king in detail.
Then, hearing what the messenger said, Shumbha of fearful command angrily said to his general Dhumraksha, best of the strong:

Dhumraksha, some beautiful woman is on the snowy mountain; go quickly and bring her so that she comes here.

The Goddess said: "Hero, you have been sent by the king of the daityas; if you kill me, what can I do to you? But I consider going impossible without a battle."

Go to the netherworld, or fight if you have the strength." Hearing these infuriating words, they said to one another:

Rutting elephants like dark mountains spread their trumpeting through the battle; camels too, like small hills, raised gurgling cries from their throats.
Horses bred in lofty lands neighed, with broad neck-ornaments, skilled in their paces; setting their hooves on the heads of elephants, they flew along the path of the sky like birds.
Seeing the enemy's army thus advancing, Ambika strung her bow and rang her bell, which brings despair to foes; the lion too roared, shaking its mane.
Then Nishumbha, seeing Shiva standing on the snowy mountain with lovely ornaments and weapons, spoke words full of feeling, like one skilled in the ways of dalliance:
On a lovely body such as yours even a scattered jasmine petal causes pain; how, great queen, will you wage fearful battle with that charming body?
Having spoken thus, the great asura fell silent, and Chandika said to him: "Why do you talk in vain, foolish asura? Fight, or else go to the abode of the nagas."
Then the great chariot-warrior, furious, sent a wondrous shower of arrows in battle, as dense clouds pour down water on the battlefield when the rains have come.
With sharp arrows, tridents, axes, slings, iron clubs, bows, bhushundis, darts, razor-headed arrows and great swords, the proud ones fought.
In that battle great elephants like black mountains reeled about, their temples split; and the banners of Shumbha and Nishumbha, white as flocks of cranes, lay broken and fallen.
Daityas with bodies torn apart like fish, headless horses, terrible to see — in the battle Kalika deprived them of life, and other asuras became the lion's prey.
Rivers of blood flowed in the midst of it, heaped with the slain; the warriors' hair was like water-weed, and their upper garments like white foam.

Horseman fell upon horseman, elephant-rider upon those mounted on elephants, chariot-warrior upon chariot-warrior, and foot soldier upon foot soldiers; there was a great strife of equal against equal.
Then Nishumbha reflected in his heart: "A dreadful time has come now. By an adverse time a poor man may become very rich, and a very rich man poor;
a dullard may become of brilliant mind and a great mind dull; the cruel may be praised by many; the mighty suffer defeat in battle, and the weak conquer at the forefront of war.
Victory or defeat comes to embodied beings effortlessly, by the will of the supreme Lord. Not even Maheshvara, the lotus-born or the lord of Rama could live by overstepping time.
Having come to the front of battle, heroes do not approve of flight in their hearts. But how can victory over her be won in battle, since my whole army has been destroyed?
Surely she has come to accomplish the gods' work and to crush the daityas' strength; she is the ancient form, the supreme nature, Shiva — never an ordinary woman.
Even death at a woman's hands is declared inglorious by those who would taste the flavour of battle; yet without fighting, how shall we show our faces before the king of the asuras?"

Having reflected thus, the great chariot-warrior mounted his huge chariot, urged on by the charioteer, and went swiftly to where the consort of Maheshvara was, the bloom of whose youth the wives of the gods longed for.

His sword broken, he sank an arrow into the breast of the supreme Mother, and she cut that too; again he hurled a trident at her heart, and she smashed it with a blow of her fist.
Taking up a mace, the great chariot-warrior, the asura facing death, rushed again at the Mother; she crushed it with the edge of her trident, and with another trident she tore him apart.
Then Ambika, with her sharp arrows like terrible serpents, fit to drink the blood of the gods' foes, smeared with poison, slew Nishumbha and brought him to the ground.
When his younger brother of immeasurable strength had been felled, the lord of the asuras, filled with rage, standing in his chariot and bearing eight arms, went to where the consort of the Lord was.
Then he blew his conch, the subduer of foes, and made an unbearable twang of his bowstring; the lion too roared, shaking its mane, and the sky resounded with the three sounds.
Then the Mother of the world laughed aloud, and all the enemies of the gods trembled at it; the gods raised the cry "Victory!" when Ambika said, "Stand firm in battle."
The sage said: Hearing, O king, that these chief daityas had been slain, the great asura of mighty valour commanded his own invincible hosts, who rejoiced at the very mention of war:

The king of the daityas hurled a great spear with a blazing point, and she struck it down with a firebrand. Shiva split the arrows shot by Shumbha, and he too split the arrows loosed by Shiva a thousandfold.
Chandika raised her trident and struck the great asura; he fell unconscious, like a mountain whose wings have been cut off by Indra, shaking heaven, earth and ocean.
Then, bearing the pain caused by the trident, the mighty one put forth ten thousand arms and struck Kalika, the great Goddess with her lion, with discuses that could destroy the immortals.
She playfully split his discuses, raised her trident and struck the asura; having received death from Shiva's lotus hand, which purifies the world, the two brothers reached the supreme abode.
When the mighty Nishumbha of terrible valour and Shumbha had been slain, all the daityas entered Bali's abode.

This whole world, moving and unmoving, is woven through and through in me alone, the support of all; I move the entire world."

Then the wind made an effort with all his strength; when it did not stir from its place, he was ashamed.

I am Viranchi the creator, I am Achyuta the protector of the world, I am Rudra the destroyer; I bewilder the whole universe.

who, seeing our most unbearable power, fled in fear to the abode of the nagas, crying 'Run, run!'?

in these and other holy lands, or in any place whatever, one who has an abode of the Mother built is freed from bondage.
